claims.text: Standard boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment undergo measurable molten-aluminum corrosion at about 660°C.
Lanthanum can be incorporated into the boride-based material during synthesis as a single-step composition modification.
Adding lanthanum to boride-based alloys will improve their resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
Lanthanum segregates to grain boundaries and interfaces in the boride-based alloy.
Segregated lanthanum promotes in situ formation of a protective oxide such as La2O3 on the component surface.
Lanthanum doping causes a stable and adherent oxide barrier to form during high-temperature exposure.
Formation of a surface metal-oxide or passivating layer can improve an alloy's corrosion resistance.
The proposed oxide barrier slows diffusion and reaction of molten aluminum with the boride-based material.
Lanthanum-doped boride-based components will have a significantly lower corrosion rate than otherwise identical undoped components.
The predicted corrosion improvement can be quantified through reduced mass loss and lower corrosion current density.
The beneficial effect should persist near 660°C in the chemical environment typical of molten-aluminum hot-dip plating.
Effectiveness requires a lanthanum concentration that produces a continuous protective oxide without creating unwanted secondary phases.
The optimal lanthanum dosage is not yet quantified.
The magnitude of the expected corrosion-rate reduction is not yet quantified.
The long-term stability of the doped oxide layer under cyclic thermal stress remains unvalidated.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement, exemplified by at least a 30% corrosion-rate reduction or comparable oxide-stability improvement, would falsify the hypothesis.
